title: Popular Cultures of Contemporary East Asia

sections.note: This course is a general survey of Chinese civilization, combining history, literature, philosophy, and culture. Content covers a wide range of topics, including geography and historical heritage; intellectual traditions of Confucianism, Legalism, Daoism, and Buddhism; poetry, fiction, drama, and art; popular belief and culture; family, gender, and sexuality; rituals and ceremonies; and food and everyday life. Readings draw on both scholarly work and translated Chinese writings, alongside an examination of material culture such as bronze vessels, ceramics, painting, calligraphy, and fashion.

Samurai, ninja, sushi, geisha, manga, anime, Nintendo, Mt. Fuji, kimono, haiku, tea ceremony, Zen, Shinto, washoku, umami, high-tech, modesty, harmony with nature, and four seasons. These are some of the things that may come to your mind when you think about Japanese culture. Indeed, many people in Japan also perceive them as characterizing Japanese culture, often calling them “cool.” This course examines Japanese culture by looking through its perceived images and investigating its historical development. We will traverse several centuries of Japanese history and explore various facets of Japanese culture. Through this exploration, you will develop appreciation of the ever-changing complexity of Japanese culture and society, and a critical perspective from which you can analyze ways in which a culture and cultural identity are defined and redefined within the contexts of history, societies, economics, politics, religions, belief systems, and ideologies.

This course invites students to explore modern East Asian history and culture through the perspectives of underrepresented communities—disabled individuals, LGBTQ+ activists, Indigenous people, migrant laborers, and others whose stories are often absent from mainstream accounts of economic “miracles” and Cold War geopolitics. Instead of focusing solely on state actors, the course centers the lived experiences of those whose voices have been sidelined by imperialism, patriarchy, and systemic discrimination.

This course aims at an interdisciplinary study of the visual culture of major sacred sites in Japan. It will examine the art and architecture of sacred sites and position them within a variety of contexts. Particular emphasis will be placed on the ways in which the art and architecture are/were used in rituals. The types of sacred sites to be studied include: imperial mausolea, capitals, Buddhist temples, Shinto shrines, warrior castles, tea houses, mountains and fields, and parks. Through successfully completing this course, students will enrich their understanding of the roles of the art and architecture in sacred sites against the background of their historical, cultural, religious, political, and social significance. It also covers today’s controversial issues related to Japanese sacred sites.

This course is designed to offer students the opportunity to develop their skills and methods in translating texts from Korean into English. This course is intended for students who are interested in deepening their knowledge of the Korean language and translation. Students will practice reading and translating various types of Korean texts which include novels, cartoons, movie/drama subtitles, and newspaper articles based on the foundation they learned in Korean language courses. Students will analyze translated works before they translate and discuss how to approach translating various genres depending on their targeted audiences, purposes, and circumstances. The course will conclude with a translation project, in which students select a work of their interests to translate and write a brief paper about their approach to the texts they have chosen. sections.note: Cinema and Machines in the Age of A.I.: Asian Intelligence Artificial intelligence is transforming how images are made, circulated, and understood. But what if cinema has been teaching machines how to see all along—and has itself been inspired by machines in return? This interdisciplinary course examines the intertwined histories of cinema, machines, and artificial intelligence through the lens of Global Asian media cultures. Moving beyond familiar narratives of technological innovation, students investigate how the Chinese-speaking world and the broader Asia-Pacific have become central sites of AI development, media infrastructure, and cross-cultural imagination. Drawing on film and media studies, Global Asian studies, critical AI studies, science and technology studies (STS), and digital humanities, the course explores topics including machine vision, automation, surveillance, labor, techno-orientalism, algorithmic policing, content moderation, AI-generated art, and emerging AI-driven filmmaking practices. Through films, contemporary artworks, hands-on AI experimentation, and critical scholarship, students develop humanistic approaches to understanding—and creatively engaging with—the political, aesthetic, and ethical futures of artificial intelligence within the long history of moving image media and screen cultures. Designed for upper-level undergraduate and graduate students, the course culminates in an original research paper or a research-based creative project tailored to each student's interests.

The aim of this course is to enable advanced learners of Korean to understand and discuss topics of Korean culture, politics, and society, based on readings of various sources (e.g., newspapers, contemporary journal articles) as well as media materials. These reading and media materials serve as the foundation for classroom activities and projects which will help bring their conversation/discussion skills and writing ability to an advanced-high or professional level. This section is offered through the BTAA Course Share Program and will be video-conference/Zoom/online taught by Ohio State University.

sections.note: In this course we will study the principles of Indian religious art through a selection of primary and secondary readings, and a vast collection of images. We will learn to identify the different structures and styles of Indian sacred buildings of the classical and medieval periods, and we will explore how they served their religious purposes. Also, we will study some of the masterpieces of Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain art, highlighting the social status and agency of the artists who created them.

sections.note: In this course, we will examine the history, philosophy, and physical practices of yoga throughout its two-thousand-year development in South Asia. We will also investigate the ritual practices of yoga that found root in South Asia, but that eventually spread to Europe and North America as a type of secular physical exercise.

sections.note: Course title: Death, Dying and the Dead in Japanese Buddhism Course description: From its inception, the Buddhist tradition has shown an abiding concern for death, the dying and the dead. This upper level seminar will examine the doctrinal and symbolic meanings of death, the ritual and meditative practices of the dying, as well as the treatment of the dead in the context of Japanese Buddhism. Drawing on recent secondary scholarship, we will examine the interface between doctrine and social practice in deathbed rituals, funerary practices and memorial services, the material, visual and literary culture of the dying and the dead, and the ethical and societal issues concerning death, dying and the dead in Japan.

sections.note: Description: This graduate seminar examines major themes and historiographical debates in Chinese history from the Neolithic period to 1800. Through critical reading and discussion of secondary sources, students will engage key scholarship and put historical perspectives in conversation with one another. Course topics include the origins of Chinese civilization, political evolution from the pre-imperial to early imperial eras, the Tang-Song transition, intellectual traditions, religions, textual production and manuscript culture, gender and sexuality, ethnicity and conquest dynasties, Chinese law and medicine, and socio-economic and environmental histories.
